claim: Data mining of RNA-Seq analysis of CD14+ monocytes showed enrichment for metabolic and hypoxia inducible factor (HIF) pathways in sarcoidosis.
source: Data mining of our RNA-Seq analysis of CD14+monocytes showed enrichment for metabolic and hypoxia inducible factor (HIF) pathways in sarcoidosis.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis showing pathway enrichment

claim: Sarcoidosis macrophages and monocytes exhibit higher protein levels for HIF-α isoforms, HIF-1β, and their transcriptional co-activator p300.
source: Further investigation revealed that sarcoidosis macrophages and monocytes exhibit higher protein levels for HIF-α isoforms, HIF-1β, and their transcriptional co-activator p300 as well as glucose transporter 1 (Glut1).
evidence: Based on western blot and protein expression data presented in the manuscript

claim: Sarcoidosis macrophages and monocytes exhibit higher protein levels for glucose transporter 1 (Glut1).
source: Further investigation revealed that sarcoidosis macrophages and monocytes exhibit higher protein levels for HIF-α isoforms, HIF-1β, and their transcriptional co-activator p300 as well as glucose transporter 1 (Glut1).
evidence: Based on western blot data showing Glut1 protein expression

claim: In situ hybridization of sarcoidosis granulomatous lung tissues showed abundance of HIF-1α in the center of granulomas.
source: In situ hybridization of sarcoidosis granulomatous lung tissues showed abundance of HIF-1α in the center of granulomas.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data from tissue samples

claim: Targeted down regulation of HIF-1α via short interfering RNA decreased IL-1β and IL-17 production.
source: The abundance of HIF isoforms was mechanistically linked to elevated IL-1β and IL-17 since targeted down regulation of HIF-1α via short interfering RNA or a HIF-1α inhibitor decreased their production.
evidence: Based on siRNA knockdown experiments showing decreased cytokine production

claim: A HIF-1α inhibitor decreased IL-1β and IL-17 production.
source: The abundance of HIF isoforms was mechanistically linked to elevated IL-1β and IL-17 since targeted down regulation of HIF-1α via short interfering RNA or a HIF-1α inhibitor decreased their production.
evidence: Based on pharmacological inhibition experiments showing decreased cytokine production

claim: Chloroquine, a lysosomal inhibitor, decreased lysosomal associated protein 2 (LAMP2) and HIF-1α levels.
source: Pharmacological intervention using chloroquine, a lysosomal inhibitor, decreased lysosomal associated protein 2 (LAMP2) and HIF-1α levels and modified cytokine production.
evidence: Based on western blot data showing decreased protein levels after chloroquine treatment

claim: Chloroquine modified cytokine production in sarcoidosis cells.
source: Pharmacological intervention using chloroquine, a lysosomal inhibitor, decreased lysosomal associated protein 2 (LAMP2) and HIF-1α levels and modified cytokine production.
evidence: Based on ELISA measurements of cytokines after chloroquine treatment

claim: Increased activity of HIF-α isoforms regulate Th1/Th17 mediated inflammation in sarcoidosis.
source: These data suggest that increased activity of HIF-α isoforms regulate Th1/Th17 mediated inflammation in sarcoidosis.
evidence: Based on multiple experimental results showing correlation between HIF-α and Th1/Th17 cytokines

claim: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown etiology characterized by extensive local inflammation and granuloma formation in different organs with an increase in T-helper type 1 (Th1) mediated cytokine production.
source: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown etiology that is characterized by extensive local inflammation and granuloma formation in different organs with an increase in T-helper type 1 (Th1) mediated cytokine production (Hunninghake et al., 1994; Iannuzzi et al., 2007; Miyara et al., 2006; Rastogi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations describing sarcoidosis characteristics

claim: Pulmonary involvement in sarcoidosis is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality.
source: Pulmonary involvement in sarcoidosis is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge about sarcoidosis

claim: In the lungs, the presence of activated macrophages and the expansion of oligoclonal T and B cells suggest sustained activation of inflammatory pathways in sarcoidosis.
source: In the lungs, the presence of activated macrophages and the expansion of oligoclonal T and B cells suggest sustained activation of inflammatory pathways in this disease (Fazel et al., 1992; Iannuzzi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing immune cell characteristics in sarcoidosis

claim: Activated macrophages, monocytes, and T cells in sarcoidosis produce a plethora of cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1β, interferon (IFN) gamma, IL-17, and others.
source: Activated macrophages, monocytes, and T cells in sarcoidosis produce a plethora of cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1β, interferon (IFN) gamma, IL-17, and others (Facco et al., 2011; Müller-Quernheim, 1998; Rastogi et al., 2011; Talreja et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations describing cytokine production in sarcoidosis

claim: Sarcoidosis bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cells and alveolar macrophages (AMs) exhibit high constitutively active p38 and lack dual specificity phosphatase (DUSP1 or MKP-1).
source: Previously, we have shown that sarcoidosis bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cells and alveolar macrophages (AMs), unlike those from healthy controls, exhibit high constitutively active p38 and lack dual specificity phosphatase (DUSP1 or MKP-1).
evidence: Based on previous work by the authors cited in the manuscript

claim: The sustained p38 activation directly controls expression of several cytokines in sarcoidosis AMs and monocytes.
source: The sustained p38 activation directly controls expression of several cytokines in sarcoidosis AMs and monocytes and the modulation of p38 regulates T cell responses (Rastogi et al., 2011; Talreja et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by previous work by the authors

claim: The modulation of p38 regulates T cell responses in sarcoidosis.
source: The sustained p38 activation directly controls expression of several cytokines in sarcoidosis AMs and monocytes and the modulation of p38 regulates T cell responses (Rastogi et al., 2011; Talreja et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by previous work by the authors

claim: RNA-sequencing in sarcoidosis monocytes identified altered gene expression profiles and cellular pathways including metabolic, glycolysis and lipolysis, phagocytosis, inflammation, oxidative phosphorylation, and HIF signaling pathways.
source: Recently, we performed RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) in sarcoidosis monocytes and identified altered gene expression profiles and cellular pathways (Talreja et al., 2017). These were: metabolic including glycolysis and lipolysis, phagocytosis, inflammation, oxidative phosphorylation, and HIF signaling pathways (Talreja et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data from previous work by the authors

claim: A large number of differentially expressed genes in sarcoidosis monocytes contain hypoxia response elements (HREs) in their regulatory regions.
source: Among differentially expressed genes in sarcoidosis monocytes, we found a large number of genes containing hypoxia response elements (HREs) in their regulatory regions and, by pathway analysis, enrichment of hypoxia inducible factor signaling pathways.
evidence: Based on bioinformatic analysis of RNA-seq data

claim: Pathway analysis showed enrichment of hypoxia inducible factor signaling pathways in sarcoidosis monocytes.
source: Among differentially expressed genes in sarcoidosis monocytes, we found a large number of genes containing hypoxia response elements (HREs) in their regulatory regions and, by pathway analysis, enrichment of hypoxia inducible factor signaling pathways.
evidence: Based on pathway analysis of RNA-seq data

claim: 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)-based analysis identified metabolic and mitochondrial alterations in sarcoidosis.
source: Furthermore, in an independent study applying 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)-based analysis, we identified metabolic and mitochondrial alterations in sarcoidosis (Geamanu et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on NMR analysis from previous work by the authors

claim: HIF-isoform expression plays an important role in the maintenance of inflammation in sarcoidosis.
source: Based on these observations, we hypothesize that HIF-isoform expression plays an important role in the maintenance of inflammation (Rastogi et al., 2011; Talreja et al., 2016), metabolic imbalance, and mitochondrial dysfunction in sarcoidosis (Geamanu et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis based on previous observations

claim: HIF-isoform expression plays an important role in metabolic imbalance in sarcoidosis.
source: Based on these observations, we hypothesize that HIF-isoform expression plays an important role in the maintenance of inflammation (Rastogi et al., 2011; Talreja et al., 2016), metabolic imbalance, and mitochondrial dysfunction in sarcoidosis (Geamanu et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis based on previous observations

claim: HIF-isoform expression plays an important role in mitochondrial dysfunction in sarcoidosis.
source: Based on these observations, we hypothesize that HIF-isoform expression plays an important role in the maintenance of inflammation (Rastogi et al., 2011; Talreja et al., 2016), metabolic imbalance, and mitochondrial dysfunction in sarcoidosis (Geamanu et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis based on previous observations

claim: HIF-1α and HIF-2α are key transcriptional regulators of hypoxia-associated genes to adapt to decreased availability of O2.
source: The oxygen-sensitive transcription factors HIF-1α and HIF-2α are key transcriptional regulators of hypoxia-associated genes to adapt to decreased availability of O2 (Semenza, 2011; Wang and Green, 2012).
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing HIF function

claim: In the presence of O2, cytosolic HIF-α isoforms are hydroxylated by prolyl-hydroxylases (PHD) through an iron dependent mechanism.
source: In the presence of O2, cytosolic HIF-α isoforms are hydroxylated by prolyl-hydroxylases (PHD) through an iron dependent mechanism, which prevents heterodimerization with HIF-1β (ARNT) and consequent nuclear translocation as an active transcription factor (Palazon et al., 2014; Semenza, 2003; Semenza, 2011).
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing HIF regulation

claim: Hydroxylation of HIF-α isoforms prevents heterodimerization with HIF-1β (ARNT) and consequent nuclear translocation as an active transcription factor.
source: In the presence of O2, cytosolic HIF-α isoforms are hydroxylated by prolyl-hydroxylases (PHD) through an iron dependent mechanism, which prevents heterodimerization with HIF-1β (ARNT) and consequent nuclear translocation as an active transcription factor (Palazon et al., 2014; Semenza, 2003; Semenza, 2011).
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing HIF regulation

claim: HIF transcription factors alter the expression of various genes involved in metabolism, cell differentiation, proliferation, and angiogenesis in hypoxic tissues.
source: HIF transcription factors alter the expression of various genes involved in metabolism, cell differentiation, proliferation, and angiogenesis in hypoxic tissues.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about HIF function

claim: Under normoxic conditions, sarcoidosis AMs and monocytes show enhanced expression and activity of HIF-1α.
source: Under normoxic conditions we found enhanced expression and activity of HIF-1α in sarcoidosis AMs and monocytes.
evidence: Based on western blot and functional assay data from the study

claim: HIF-1α expression was directly correlated with IL-1β production in AMs and PBMCs.
source: Furthermore, HIF-1α expression was directly correlated with IL-1β production in AMs and PBMCs.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of protein expression and cytokine production data

claim: Down regulation of HIF-1α expression via siRNA decreased IL-1β in sarcoidosis AMs.
source: Down regulation of HIF-1α expression via short interfering RNA (siRNA) decreased IL-1β in sarcoidosis AMs, while decreased HIF-1α expression in PBMCs decreased IL-1β and IL-17 in response to anti-CD3 challenge.
evidence: Based on siRNA knockdown experiments measuring IL-1β production

claim: Decreased HIF-1α expression in PBMCs decreased IL-1β and IL-17 in response to anti-CD3 challenge.
source: Down regulation of HIF-1α expression via short interfering RNA (siRNA) decreased IL-1β in sarcoidosis AMs, while decreased HIF-1α expression in PBMCs decreased IL-1β and IL-17 in response to anti-CD3 challenge.
evidence: Based on siRNA knockdown experiments measuring cytokine production after anti-CD3 stimulation

claim: Patients enrolled in the study were ambulatory outpatients who were not hypoxic.
source: Patients (Table 1 and Materials and methods) were ambulatory outpatients who were not hypoxic.
evidence: Based on patient selection criteria and clinical characteristics

claim: There are clear differences in the intensity and expression of genes related to the HIF pathway in monocytes of healthy controls and sarcoidosis subjects.
source: There are clear differences in the intensity and expression of genes related to the HIF pathway in monocytes of healthy controls and sarcoidosis subjects.
evidence: Based on heatmap visualization of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A

claim: ARNT (HIF-1β) heterodimerizes with HIF-1α to form a transcriptional active complex.
source: The transcription factor aryl hydrocarbon receptor nuclear translocator (ARNT, also known as HIF-1β) heterodimerizes with HIF-1α to form a transcriptional active complex (Wolff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by literature citation describing ARNT function

claim: Sarcoidosis monocytes demonstrate significantly higher ARNT gene expression compared to healthy controls.
source: The gene count between sarcoidosis and healthy control subjects demonstrate significantly higher ARNT gene expression in sarcoidosis monocytes (Figure 1B).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq gene count data shown in Figure 1B

claim: EPAS1 (HIF-2α) is a hypoxia inducible transcription factor.
source: Endothelial PAS domain protein 1 (EPAS1), also known as HIF-2α, is a hypoxia inducible transcription factor (Hu et al., 2003; Thompson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing EPAS1/HIF-2α function

claim: Sarcoidosis monocytes demonstrate significantly higher EPAS1 expression compared to healthy controls.
source: The EPAS1 gene count between sarcoidosis and healthy control subjects demonstrates significantly higher EPAS1 expression in sarcoidosis monocytes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq gene count data shown in Figure 1C

claim: EP300 is a co-activator important for transcriptional activity of HIFs.
source: EP300 is a co-activator important for transcriptional activity of HIFs (Palazon et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by literature citation describing p300 function

claim: Sarcoidosis monocytes show higher p300 gene expression compared to healthy controls.
source: Similarly, we found higher p300 gene expression in sarcoidosis monocytes as compared to healthy controls (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq gene count data shown in Figure 1D

claim: There were no differences in HIF-1α gene transcripts between sarcoidosis and control monocytes.
source: However, there were no differences in HIF-1α gene transcripts between the two groups.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq gene count analysis

claim: HIF-1α is known to be predominantly regulated through modification of its protein stability.
source: Since HIF-1α is known to be predominantly regulated through modification of its protein stability (Lee et al., 2004; Salceda and Caro, 1997), we evaluated HIF-1α and HIF-2α protein abundance in AMs and monocytes of sarcoidosis patients, isolated as described in Materials and methods.
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing HIF-1α regulation

claim: Sarcoidosis AMs show increased HIF-1α protein expression compared to healthy controls under normoxic conditions.
source: Western analysis of cell lysates probed with antibody against HIF-1α showed increased HIF-1α protein expression in sarcoidosis AMs and monocytes (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Based on western blot data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: Sarcoidosis monocytes show increased HIF-1α protein expression compared to healthy controls under normoxic conditions.
source: Western analysis of cell lysates probed with antibody against HIF-1α showed increased HIF-1α protein expression in sarcoidosis AMs and monocytes (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Based on western blot data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: Sarcoidosis AMs show increased HIF-2α protein expression compared to healthy controls.
source: Similar results were seen for HIF-2α protein expression (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Based on western blot data shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: HIFα heterodimerizes with ARNT (HIF-1β), translocates to the nucleus, and recruits transcriptional coactivator p300 to transactivate target genes containing hypoxia-responsive elements (HREs).
source: Since HIFα heterodimerizes with ARNT (also known as HIF-1β), translocates to the nucleus, and recruits transcriptional coactivator p300 to transactivate target genes containing hypoxia-responsive elements (HREs) (Semenza, 2003; Talwar et al., 2017a; Talwar et al., 2017b), we also examined their protein expression.
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing HIF transcriptional mechanism

claim: Sarcoidosis AMs show higher expression of ARNT compared to healthy controls.
source: Sarcoidosis AMs also show a higher expression of ARNT (Figure 2E and F) and p300 (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: Based on western blot data shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: Sarcoidosis AMs show higher expression of p300 compared to healthy controls.
source: Sarcoidosis AMs also show a higher expression of ARNT (Figure 2E and F) and p300 (Figure 2E and G).
evidence: Based on western blot data shown in Figure 2E and G

claim: Isolated monocytes from sarcoidosis subjects show significantly higher HIF-1α protein expression compared to healthy controls.
source: Similarly, we evaluated the HIF-1α protein abundance in isolated monocytes from sarcoidosis subjects and healthy controls and found significantly higher HIF-1α expression (Figure 2H and I).
evidence: Based on western blot data shown in Figure 2H and I

claim: HIF-2α was not detected in either sarcoidosis or control monocytes at the protein level by western blot.
source: However, in contrast to increased HIF-2α gene transcripts, we did not detect HIF-2α in either sarcoidosis or control monocytes at the protein level.
evidence: Based on western blot analysis showing no detectable HIF-2α protein

claim: In healthy controls 5–9% of PBMCs are CD14+HIF-1α+, whereas in sarcoidosis 20% to 35% of PBMCs are CD14+HIF-1α+.
source: FACS analysis of PBMCs double stained for CD14 and HIF-1α or HIF-2α shows that in healthy controls 5–9% of PBMCs are CD14+HIF-1α+, whereas in sarcoidosis 20% to 35% of PBMCs are CD14+ HIF-1α+.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2K

claim: In healthy controls 25–60% of CD14+ monocytes are HIF-1α+, whereas in sarcoidosis 64–96% of CD14+ monocytes are HIF-1α+.
source: Analysis of CD14+ monocytes based on the expression of HIF-1α shows 25–60% HIF-1α+ CD14+ monocytes in controls, whereas in sarcoidosis HIF-1α+ CD14+ monocytes are 64–96% (K).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2K

claim: In healthy controls 0–0.1% of PBMCs are CD14+HIF-2α+, whereas in sarcoidosis 1–3% of PBMCs are CD14+HIF-2α+.
source: Interestingly, in healthy controls 0–0.1% of PBMCs are CD14+ HIF-2α+, whereas in sarcoidosis 1–3% of PBMCs are CD14+ HIF-2α+.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2L

claim: In healthy controls the percentage of HIF-2α+ CD14+ monocytes is negligible, whereas in sarcoidosis there is higher percentage of HIF-2α+ CD14+ monocytes (5–9%).
source: It shows that in healthy controls the percentage of HIF-2α+ CD14+ monocytes is negligible, whereas in sarcoidosis there is higher percentage of HIF-2α+ CD14+monocytes (5–9%) (Figure 2L).
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2L

claim: Sarcoidosis AMs and peripheral monocytes exhibit increased expression of HIF isoforms compared to healthy controls.
source: Thus, these results show that sarcoidosis AMs and peripheral monocytes exhibit increased expression of HIF isoforms compared to healthy controls.
evidence: Based on multiple protein expression and flow cytometry data

claim: HIF-2α shows a different protein expression profile in lung macrophages versus peripheral monocytes with low abundance in monocytes versus AMs.
source: These data suggest a different protein expression profile of HIF-2α in lung macrophages versus peripheral monocytes with low abundance in monocytes versus AMs.
evidence: Based on comparison of western blot and flow cytometry data between AMs and monocytes

claim: About 60–90% of sarcoidosis AMs express HIF-1α.
source: We quantitated the percentage of cells showing HIF-1α expression (Figure 3A and B) in sarcoidosis. The staining is representative of one out of the five patients. It shows that about 60–90% of AMs express HIF-1α.
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence quantitation shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: Confocal microscopy images show nuclear and cytoplasmic accumulation of HIF-1α in sarcoidosis AMs.
source: Confocal microscopy images show nuclei stained with DAPI (blue) in a single AM (C) and a multinucleated giant cell (D), nuclear and cytoplasmic accumulation of HIF-1α in green (E and F), overlay image shows nuclear co-localization of HIF-1α (G and H).
evidence: Based on confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 3C-H

claim: Enhanced expression and accumulation of HIF-1α occurs in the cytoplasm and nuclei of sarcoidosis AMs, both in a single AM and in a multinucleated giant cell.
source: We saw enhanced expression and accumulation of HIF-1α in the cytoplasm and nuclei of sarcoidosis AMs, both in a single AM (Figure 3E) and in a multinucleated giant cell (Figure 3F) that are known to be characteristic cells in sarcoidosis granuloma.
evidence: Based on confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 3E and F

claim: HIF-1α is highly expressed and accumulates in nuclei compared to cytoplasm in sarcoidosis AMs.
source: HIF-1α is highly expressed and overlay images show that HIF-1α accumulates in nuclei (Figure 3G and H) as compared to cytoplasm.
evidence: Based on confocal microscopy overlay images shown in Figure 3G and H

claim: Positive immunostaining for HIF-1α was seen in multinucleated giant cells of granulomas as well as macrophages in sarcoidosis lung biopsies.
source: Positive immunostaining was seen in multinucleated giant cells of granulomas as well as macrophages (Figure 3I and J, thick arrow), whereas fibroblasts and normal lungs lack HIF-1α expression.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3I and J

claim: Fibroblasts and normal lungs lack HIF-1α expression.
source: Positive immunostaining was seen in multinucleated giant cells of granulomas as well as macrophages (Figure 3I and J, thick arrow), whereas fibroblasts and normal lungs lack HIF-1α expression.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry data showing absence of staining in fibroblasts and normal lung

claim: Increased HIF-1α immunostaining signal was observed in sarcoidosis liver and skin tissue samples.
source: Similarly, we observed increased HIF-1α immunostaining signal in sarcoidosis liver and skin tissue samples.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry data from liver and skin tissues

claim: HIF-1α is a critical transcription factor regulating metabolic reprogramming during inflammation, in part through upregulation of the SLC2A1 gene encoding glucose transporter (Glut)1.
source: HIF-1α is a critical transcription factor regulating metabolic reprogramming during inflammation, in part through upregulation of the SLC2A1 gene encoding glucose transporter (Glut)1 (Chen et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by literature citation describing HIF-1α regulation of Glut1

claim: HIF-1α and Glut1 upregulation contribute to production of several pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β.
source: HIF-1α and Glut1 upregulation contribute to production of several pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β (Talwar et al., 2017a; Talwar et al., 2017b; Tannahill et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing HIF-1α and Glut1 effects on cytokine production

claim: Sarcoidosis AMs exhibited a variable amount of Glut1 and pro-IL-1β (18/18 patients) but only 1 out of 10 healthy controls showed expression.
source: Sarcoidosis AMs exhibited a variable amount of Glut1 and pro-IL-1β (18/18 patients) but only 1 out of 10 healthy controls showed expression (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Based on western blot data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: Increased pro-IL-1β expression directly correlated with Glut1 and HIF-1α expression in sarcoidosis AMs.
source: Furthermore, increased pro-IL-1β expression directly correlated with Glut1 and HIF-1α expression in sarcoidosis AMs (Figure 4E).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E

claim: Unstimulated and LPS-stimulated cultured sarcoidosis AMs secrete higher IL-1β compared to healthy controls.
source: The results showed that unstimulated and LPS-stimulated cultured sarcoidosis AMs and monocytes secrete higher IL-1β as compared to healthy controls (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Unstimulated and LPS-stimulated cultured sarcoidosis monocytes secrete higher IL-1β compared to healthy controls.
source: The results showed that unstimulated and LPS-stimulated cultured sarcoidosis AMs and monocytes secrete higher IL-1β as compared to healthy controls (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 4G

claim: Increased expression of HIF-1α leads to increased IL-1β production in sarcoidosis patients.
source: These data suggest that increased expression of HIF-1α leads to increased IL-1β production in sarcoidosis patients.
evidence: Based on correlation and functional data showing relationship between HIF-1α and IL-1β

claim: IL-1Ra (IL-1RII) competitively binds to IL-1β and forms a nonsignaling complex to inhibit the effect of IL-1β on cells.
source: IL-1Ra (IL-1RII) competitively binds to IL-1β and forms a nonsignaling complex IL-1Ra to the surface receptors for IL-1β and inhibits the effect of IL-1β on cells (Arend, 2000; Janson et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing IL-1Ra function

claim: Sarcoidosis AMs produced significantly high levels of IL-1Ra compared to control AMs.
source: Figure 4H shows that sarcoidosis AMs produced significantly high levels of IL-1Ra as compared to control AMs.
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 4H

claim: Sarcoidosis PBMCs produced high levels of IL-1Ra compared to control PBMCs.
source: Similarly, sarcoidosis PBMCs (Figure 4I) produced high levels of IL-1Ra as compared to control PBMCs.
evidence: Based on ELISA data shown in Figure 4I

claim: IL-1β is regulated at the transcriptional level through expression of several transcription factors including STAT3, HIF-1α, and others.
source: IL-1β is regulated at the transcriptional level through expression of several transcription factors including Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription (STAT) 3, HIF-1α, and others (Samavati et al., 2009; Talwar et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing IL-1β transcriptional regulation

claim: Targeted downregulation of HIF-1α via siRNA of sarcoidosis AMs led to a significant reduction (about 50%) in HIF-1α protein expression.
source: Targeted downregulation of HIF-1α via siRNA of sarcoidosis AMs led to a significant reduction (about 50%) in HIF-1α (Figure 5A and B) and pro-IL-1β (Figure 5C and D) protein expression.
evidence: Based on western blot data after siRNA treatment shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: Targeted downregulation of HIF-1α via siRNA of sarcoidosis AMs led to a significant reduction in pro-IL-1β protein expression.
source: Targeted downregulation of HIF-1α via siRNA of sarcoidosis AMs led to a significant reduction (about 50%) in HIF-1α (Figure 5A and B) and pro-IL-1β (Figure 5C and D) protein expression.
evidence: Based on western blot data after siRNA treatment shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: HIF-1α siRNA significantly decreased IL-1β production in sarcoidosis AMs.
source: To determine the specificity of targeted downregulation of HIF-1α on other cytokines, we assessed the conditioned medium for IL-1β and IL-10 production and found significantly decreased IL-1β production (Figure 5E).
evidence: Based on ELISA data after siRNA treatment shown in Figure 5E

claim: HIF-1α inhibition did not inhibit IL-10 production in sarcoidosis AMs.
source: However, HIF-1α inhibition did not inhibit IL-10 production (Figure 5F).
evidence: Based on ELISA data after siRNA treatment shown in Figure 5F

claim: Targeted down regulation of HIF-1α in sarcoidosis PBMCs resulted in decreased production of IL-1β in response to LPS.
source: Similar to AMs, the targeted down regulation of HIF-1α in sarcoidosis PBMCs resulted in decreased production of IL-1β in response to LPS (Figure 6A); the effect of HIF-1α inhibition was specific for IL-1β since there was no significant effect on IL-10 production (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on ELISA data after siRNA treatment shown in Figure 6A

claim: HIF-1α inhibition had no significant effect on IL-10 production in sarcoidosis PBMCs in response to LPS.
source: Similar to AMs, the targeted down regulation of HIF-1α in sarcoidosis PBMCs resulted in decreased production of IL-1β in response to LPS (Figure 6A); the effect of HIF-1α inhibition was specific for IL-1β since there was no significant effect on IL-10 production (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on ELISA data after siRNA treatment shown in Figure 6B

claim: HIF-1α expression regulates IL-1β production in sarcoidosis AMs and PBMCs.
source: These results clearly show that HIF-1α expression regulates IL-1β production in sarcoidosis AMs and PBMCs.
evidence: Based on siRNA knockdown experiments showing decreased IL-1β after HIF-1α inhibition

claim: HIF transcription factors are key elements in the control of immune cell metabolism and function in macrophages, B-cells, and T-cells.
source: Recent work has shown that the HIF transcription factors are key elements in the control of immune cell metabolism and function in macrophages, B-cells, and T-cells (Palazon et al., 2014; Wang and Green, 2012).
evidence: Supported by literature citations describing HIF function in immune cells

claim: Th17 cells represent a lineage of effector T cells critical in host defense and autoimmunity.
source: T helper 17 cells (Th17) represent a lineage of effector T cells critical in host defense and autoimmunity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Th17 cells

claim: Th1 and Th17 cells contribute to sarcoidosis pathology.
source: It is has been shown that Th1 and Th17 cells contribute to sarcoidosis pathology (Ramstein et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by literature citation describing Th1/Th17 role in sarcoidosis

claim: Sarcoidosis PBMCs produce significantly higher levels of IL-1β compared to healthy control PBMCs in response to anti-CD3.
source: Sarcoidosis PBMCS were seen to produce significantly higher levels of IL-1β (Figure 6C) and IL-17 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on ELISA data after anti-CD3 stimulation shown in Figure 6C

claim: Sarcoidosis PBMCs produce significantly higher levels of IL-17 compared to healthy control PBMCs in response to anti-CD3.
source: Sarcoidosis PBMCS were seen to produce significantly higher levels of IL-1β (Figure 6C) and IL-17 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on ELISA data after anti-CD3 stimulation shown in Figure 6D

claim: Inhibition of HIF-1α by siRNA significantly decreased the production of anti-CD3 induced IL-1β in sarcoidosis PBMCs.
source: Inhibition of HIF-1α by siRNA significantly decreased the production of anti-CD3 induced IL-1β (Figure 6E), IL-17 (Figure 6F), and IL-6 (Figure 6G).
evidence: Based on ELISA data after siRNA treatment and anti-CD3 stimulation shown in Figure 6E

claim: Inhibition of HIF-1α by siRNA significantly decreased the production of anti-CD3 induced IL-17 in sarcoidosis PBMCs.
source: Inhibition of HIF-1α by siRNA significantly decreased the production of anti-CD3 induced IL-1β (Figure 6E), IL-17 (Figure 6F), and IL-6 (Figure 6G).
evidence: Based on ELISA data after siRNA treatment and anti-CD3 stimulation shown in Figure 6F

claim: Inhibition of HIF-1α by siRNA significantly decreased the production of anti-CD3 induced IL-6 in sarcoidosis PBMCs.
source: Inhibition of HIF-1α by siRNA significantly decreased the production of anti-CD3 induced IL-1β (Figure 6E), IL-17 (Figure 6F), and IL-6 (Figure 6G).
evidence: Based on ELISA data after siRNA treatment and anti-CD3 stimulation shown in Figure 6G

claim: Inhibition of HIF-1α did not decrease IFN-γ production in sarcoidosis PBMCs in response to anti-CD3.
source: However, inhibition of HIF-1α did not decrease IFN-γ (Figure 6H) and IL-10 (Figure 6I) production.
evidence: Based on ELISA data after siRNA treatment and anti-CD3 stimulation shown in Figure 6H

claim: Inhibition of HIF-1α did not decrease IL-10 production in sarcoidosis PBMCs in response to anti-CD3.
